quests.instruction: Deliver the pitch before the lift opens.
quests.prompt: List the feature and the benefit separately in this sentence: 'Our thermostat learns your schedule and adjusts automatically, so you save on heating without thinking about it.'
quests.correctAnswer: Feature: it learns your schedule and adjusts automatically. Benefit: you save money without having to think about it.
quests.hint: The feature is what the product does mechanically; the benefit is what changes for the person.
quests.explanation: Separating the two clearly, even just as an exercise, makes it easier to catch when a pitch has accidentally led with the feature.

quests.instruction: Deliver the pitch before the lift opens.
quests.prompt: This pitch leads with three features and no benefit: 'It has voice control, a mobile app, and geofencing.' Rewrite it leading with the single strongest benefit those features add up to.
quests.correctAnswer: It knows when you've left the house and turns the heat down before you've even reached the corner.
quests.hint: Find the one outcome all three features are really in service of.
quests.explanation: Multiple features often collapse into one real benefit - naming that benefit is more useful than listing the features that produce it.

quests.instruction: Deliver the pitch before the lift opens.
quests.prompt: A candidate keeps listing features about themselves in an interview: 'I know Python, SQL, and Tableau.' Turn that list into a benefit-led pitch for a hiring manager who mentioned messy reporting.
quests.correctAnswer: I can take your messiest spreadsheet and turn it into a report your team actually trusts by Friday.
quests.hint: Connect the specific tools to the specific problem the manager already named.
quests.explanation: Skills are features. What a manager hires for is the outcome those skills produce for their specific problem.

quests.instruction: Deliver the pitch before the lift opens.
quests.prompt: When is it stronger to open with the solution instead of the problem?
quests.correctAnswer: When the listener already clearly feels the problem, and stating it again would waste time they don't need to spend.
quests.hint: Think about what the listener already knows before you start talking.
quests.explanation: Problem-first isn't always the right order - if the problem is already obvious to the listener, leading with the solution respects their time.

quests.instruction: Deliver the pitch before the lift opens.
quests.prompt: A parent at a pediatrician's waiting room clearly already knows the problem of never remembering vaccination schedules. Pitch a reminder app to them solution-first.
quests.correctAnswer: This tracks every shot your kid needs and texts you a week before it's due, so you're never caught off guard at a checkup.
quests.hint: Skip restating a problem this listener obviously already feels - go straight to the fix.
quests.explanation: Restating an obvious problem back to someone who's living it can feel patronizing - solution-first respects what they already know.

quests.instruction: Deliver the pitch before the lift opens.
quests.prompt: Now pitch the same reminder app problem-first, to a listener at a networking event who has no kids and no prior context about vaccination schedules.
quests.correctAnswer: Parents lose track of which shots their kid's actually had - our app tracks it automatically and reminds you before every appointment.
quests.hint: This listener needs the problem stated first, since they have no existing context.
quests.explanation: The same product needs opposite structures for two different listeners - context, not a fixed rule, decides which order to use.

quests.instruction: Deliver the pitch before the lift opens.
quests.prompt: A pitch about a fitness app mentions the app's color scheme and its founding date. Does either detail serve the core message? Explain.
quests.correctAnswer: No - neither one changes what a listener understands about whether the app will actually help them, so both are safe to cut.
quests.hint: Ask whether removing the detail changes what the listener understands about the value.
quests.explanation: A useful filter for any detail: if cutting it changes nothing about the listener's understanding of the value, it wasn't serving the message.

quests.instruction: Deliver the pitch before the lift opens.
quests.prompt: This pitch has one detail that doesn't serve the message: 'Our app was founded in a small apartment two years ago and helps you track workouts with a friend for accountability.' Remove it and deliver the tightened pitch.
quests.correctAnswer: It helps you track workouts with a friend, so on the days you'd rather skip it, someone's actually expecting you to show up.
quests.hint: Cut the founding detail; keep the accountability mechanism.
quests.explanation: The founding story might be a nice detail in a longer conversation, but here it's competing for time against the actual value.

quests.instruction: Deliver the pitch before the lift opens.
quests.prompt: Write a pitch for a freelance photography business that includes zero details about camera gear or years of experience - only what changes for the client.
quests.correctAnswer: Your event gets photos back within a week, already edited, so you're not waiting a month to relive the day.
quests.hint: Focus entirely on the client's experience, not your equipment or résumé.
quests.explanation: Gear and experience are often assumed table stakes - what actually differentiates a pitch is what the client experiences differently.

quests.instruction: Deliver the pitch before the lift opens.
quests.prompt: A pitch tries to cover five loosely related benefits of a productivity app in fifteen seconds. What's the likely result?
quests.correctAnswer: The listener retains almost none of it - five competing ideas in fifteen seconds usually crowd each other out entirely.
quests.hint: Think about how much a listener can actually absorb in that short a time.
quests.explanation: Trying to say everything in too little time usually means saying nothing memorably - one clear idea beats five blurred ones.

quests.instruction: Deliver the pitch before the lift opens.
quests.prompt: From these five true benefits of a language app - offline mode, native speaker audio, gamified lessons, progress tracking, and a community forum - choose one and build a fifteen-second pitch around it for a business traveler.
quests.correctAnswer: Offline mode means you can practice on a flight with no wifi and still land ready to order dinner in the local language.
quests.hint: Match the single chosen benefit to what a business traveler specifically needs.
quests.explanation: Choosing one benefit and matching it precisely to the listener beats trying to cover the whole feature set.

quests.instruction: Deliver the pitch before the lift opens.
quests.prompt: From that same list of five, choose a different benefit and build a new fifteen-second pitch for a parent hoping their teenager sticks with a language habit.
quests.correctAnswer: The gamified lessons turn practice into something they actually want to finish, not something you have to remind them about.
quests.hint: Pick whichever benefit best addresses a parent's real worry: consistency, not features.
quests.explanation: The same five true benefits can each become the right single message, depending entirely on who's listening.

quests.instruction: Deliver the pitch before the lift opens.
quests.prompt: A pitch for a supply-chain tool says 'we optimize SKU-level inventory turnover through predictive demand forecasting.' Who might actually understand this language, and who wouldn't?
quests.correctAnswer: A warehouse operations manager might follow it; a small retail shop owner almost certainly wouldn't.
quests.hint: Ask whether the jargon is genuinely shared vocabulary for this specific listener, or just internal shorthand.
quests.explanation: Jargon isn't wrong in every context - the test is whether this particular listener actually shares the vocabulary, not whether the term is technically correct.

quests.instruction: Deliver the pitch before the lift opens.
quests.prompt: Translate that supply-chain jargon for the small retail shop owner who wouldn't follow it.
quests.correctAnswer: We predict what you'll actually sell next month, so you stop running out of your bestsellers and stop being stuck with things that don't move.
quests.hint: Describe the practical outcome in terms of what's on the shelf, not the underlying forecasting method.
quests.explanation: Translating for the listener who doesn't share the jargon is what actually makes the pitch usable, not a simplification that loses accuracy.

quests.instruction: Deliver the pitch before the lift opens.
quests.prompt: Now pitch the same predictive tool to the warehouse operations manager who does understand supply-chain terms, using appropriately technical language this time.
quests.correctAnswer: We forecast SKU-level demand a full quarter out, so reorder points adjust automatically instead of someone manually recalculating them every week.
quests.hint: This listener shares the vocabulary - use it, rather than translating unnecessarily.
quests.explanation: Simplifying for an expert audience can actually undersell you - matching the listener's real fluency is part of audience awareness too.

quests.instruction: Deliver the pitch before the lift opens.
quests.prompt: A pitch packs three numbers, two comparisons, and a technical term into one sentence. What's the risk to the listener?
quests.correctAnswer: The listener has to work hard just to follow the sentence, and that effort gets spent on parsing instead of on actually being persuaded.
quests.hint: Think about how much mental effort the listener has to spend just to understand, versus to decide.
quests.explanation: Every extra thing a listener has to track reduces how much attention is left for actually being convinced.

quests.instruction: Deliver the pitch before the lift opens.
quests.prompt: Simplify this cognitively heavy pitch: 'Our plan saves you 23% compared to Plan A and 17% compared to Plan B, with a 12-month lock-in versus their 24-month terms.' Keep only the clearest, strongest comparison.
quests.correctAnswer: You'll pay noticeably less than what you're paying now, and you're never locked in for more than a year.
quests.hint: Drop the multiple numeric comparisons and keep one simple, memorable one.
quests.explanation: One easy-to-hold comparison beats three precise ones a listener can't actually retain while standing in an elevator.

quests.instruction: Deliver the pitch before the lift opens.
quests.prompt: Simplify this pitch for a nonprofit's impact: 'We've served 4,213 families across 6 counties through 3 core programs since 2019.' Reduce it to the single clearest, most memorable idea.
quests.correctAnswer: Since we started, we've helped over four thousand families get through a hard stretch a little more easily.
quests.hint: Keep the one number that matters most and drop the rest.
quests.explanation: Precision for its own sake can overload a listener - one well-chosen number usually does more work than four stacked together.

quests.instruction: Deliver the pitch before the lift opens.
quests.prompt: 'We streamline your operations' is abstract even after simplification. What's still missing to make it concrete?
quests.correctAnswer: A specific example of one operation, before and after, showing exactly what 'streamline' means in practice.
quests.hint: 'Streamline' is still a category word - ask for the one specific thing it actually changes.
quests.explanation: Even after removing jargon, a claim can stay abstract - concreteness requires a specific before-and-after moment, not just simpler words.

quests.instruction: Deliver the pitch before the lift opens.
quests.prompt: Make 'we streamline your operations' concrete for a small logistics company, using one specific before-and-after moment.
quests.correctAnswer: Right now, confirming a delivery means three phone calls. With this, the driver taps once and everyone who needs to know already does.
quests.hint: Pick one specific task and show its before and after.
quests.explanation: The concreteness comes from picking exactly one task and following it all the way through, rather than gesturing at operations broadly.

quests.instruction: Deliver the pitch before the lift opens.
quests.prompt: A city council candidate says 'I'll improve government efficiency.' Make that concrete with one specific, believable example a resident would recognize.
quests.correctAnswer: Right now, a pothole report takes six weeks and three phone calls to even get logged. I'd make it one form, tracked publicly, start to finish.
quests.hint: Choose a specific, everyday interaction with local government a resident already recognizes.
quests.explanation: Political pitches are just as prone to abstraction as product pitches - the same concreteness technique fixes both.

quests.instruction: Deliver the pitch before the lift opens.
quests.prompt: A pitch for a car has a true but potentially distracting fact: 'it comes in eleven colors.' In a fifteen-second pitch to someone who just said they need better fuel economy, should that fact be included? Why or why not?
quests.correctAnswer: No - it's true but irrelevant to this listener's stated priority, and including it dilutes the pitch instead of strengthening it.
quests.hint: A true fact isn't automatically a fact worth including - check it against what this listener actually cares about.
quests.explanation: Not every true thing belongs in every pitch. Choosing what to leave out, deliberately, is as much a skill as choosing what to say.

quests.instruction: Deliver the pitch before the lift opens.
quests.prompt: A pitch for a job candidate includes a true but weaker credential alongside a much stronger one: 'I ran the campus coffee cart for a summer, and I also led a twelve-person team that shipped a product used by ten thousand people.' Cut the weaker detail and deliver the stronger pitch alone.
quests.correctAnswer: I led a twelve-person team that shipped a product now used by ten thousand people.
quests.hint: Including a much weaker fact next to a strong one can actually dilute the strong one - cut it.
quests.explanation: A weaker true fact placed next to a strong one doesn't add credibility - it can actually make the listener wonder why it needed mentioning.

quests.instruction: Deliver the pitch before the lift opens.
quests.prompt: A pitch for a therapy practice could mention both 'we accept most major insurance plans' and 'our founder has an unrelated hobby of woodworking.' Decide which to keep for a pitch aimed at someone hesitant about cost, and deliver it.
quests.correctAnswer: We accept most major insurance plans, so cost usually isn't the barrier people expect it to be.
quests.hint: Keep only the fact relevant to this listener's actual hesitation.
quests.explanation: Irrelevant personal color, even if charming, can crowd out the one fact that would have actually addressed the listener's real concern.

quests.instruction: Deliver the pitch before the lift opens.
quests.prompt: A job candidate is asked to explain a career gap in fifteen seconds. What should the answer prioritize: full detail, or a concise, confident framing?
quests.correctAnswer: A concise, confident framing - fifteen seconds isn't enough room for full detail, and over-explaining can read as defensive.
quests.hint: Think about what over-explaining a sensitive topic tends to signal to a listener.
quests.explanation: Brevity on a sensitive topic often reads as confidence, while over-explaining can unintentionally signal insecurity about it.

quests.instruction: Deliver the pitch before the lift opens.
quests.prompt: Write a concise, confident answer to 'so what were you doing during that year off?' for someone who spent it caring for a family member.
quests.correctAnswer: I took a year to care for a family member - it's part of why I'm particular now about actually finishing what I start.
quests.hint: Keep it brief, factual, and turn it toward a strength without over-explaining.
quests.explanation: A short, matter-of-fact answer that pivots to a strength usually lands better than a long, apologetic justification.

quests.instruction: Deliver the pitch before the lift opens.
quests.prompt: A founder is asked why their first startup failed, in a fifteen-second answer during an investor meeting. Write a concise answer that's honest without spiraling into every detail.
quests.correctAnswer: We built for a market that turned out to be too small - I learned to validate demand before writing a line of code, and that's exactly what we did this time.
quests.hint: State the core lesson briefly, then connect it to what's different now.
quests.explanation: Concise explanations of past failure work best when they name the lesson learned, not just the failure itself.

quests.instruction: Deliver the pitch before the lift opens.
quests.prompt: You're mid-pitch for a subscription meal service when the listener glances at their phone. What's the strongest way to regain their attention without being pushy?
quests.correctAnswer: Shorten what's left to the single most relevant sentence, rather than repeating yourself or raising your volume.
quests.hint: Think about what tends to re-earn attention versus what tends to lose it further.
quests.explanation: When attention starts slipping, the instinct to add more usually backfires - cutting to the sharpest remaining point works better.

quests.instruction: Deliver the pitch before the lift opens.
quests.prompt: Deliver a tightly controlled pitch for a plant-based meal delivery service in exactly two sentences, as if you know you only have that much attention left.
quests.correctAnswer: Dinner's already decided and half-cooked by the time you get home. No more staring into the fridge at seven o'clock wondering what to make.
quests.hint: Say only the two sentences that carry the entire message - nothing extra.
quests.explanation: This level tests whether you can control the whole message down to its essential shape, on demand, under real attention pressure.

quests.instruction: Deliver the pitch before the lift opens.
quests.prompt: The listener looks back up and says 'sorry, what was that?' Recover smoothly by restating your strongest single sentence, without sounding annoyed or starting over from scratch.
quests.correctAnswer: No worries - dinner shows up already half-cooked, so you're not stuck staring into the fridge at seven wondering what to make.
quests.hint: Restate your best sentence calmly, as if for the first time, rather than repeating everything you'd said before.
quests.explanation: Controlling the message means you can recover a distracted moment gracefully, because you already know exactly which sentence matters most.
